articles.title: Northampton 28-14 Gloucester: Saints come from behind to beat in-form Gloucester
articles.summary: Late tries from George Hendy and Rory Hutchison gift Northampton Saints victory over stubborn Gloucester.
articles.body:
Tries: Pearson, Langdon, Hendy, Hutchinson Cons: Belleau 4

Northampton Saints scored 28 unanswered points to come from behind and overcome a stubborn Gloucester 28-14 at DPD Stadium at Franklin's Gardens.

But England boss Steve Borthwick will be concerned after scrum-half Alex Mitchell was forced off with a hamstring injury during the first half.

Gloucester had the better of the opening exchanges with tries from Max Llewellyn and Will Joseph opening up a 14 point lead, before Tom Pearson responded for Saints.

Curtis Langdon's effort on the verge of half-time brought the scores level, but it took until the final quarter for Saints to really seize control of the game.

George Hendy added a third try after a pinpoint pass from Anthony Belleau before Rory Hutchinson's late score put the game beyond the visitors.

Victory moves Northampton up to third in the table, level on points with Gloucester in second as the Prem takes a four-week break.

Cokanasiga scores twice as Bath overcome Sale

Second-half blitz helps Saracens beat Newcastle

Quins claim victory at Exeter in nine-try nailbiter

In the misty conditions, it was the visitors who struck first.

Attacking in the Saints' 22, the returning Seb Atkinson released George Barton who offloaded to Llewellyn to dot down over the whitewash.

Saints then suffered another blow as Mitchell left the field eight days before England face Australia in the Nations Championship.

After being repeatedly repelled by Northampton's defence, Gloucester then scored again. Following a well executed set-piece move, Hendy was unable to contain Joseph, who stumbled over the line to add the Cherry and Whites' second.

Northampton desperately needed some attacking emphasis and finally found it through Pearson.

With Gloucester penalised in their own half, Saints kicked for the corner. The resulting rolling maul had seemingly come to a halt, but Langdon managed to pop the ball up to the flanker who crashed over at short range.

Saints then claimed a second in similar circumstances right before half-time. Another driving line-out was initially kept out by Gloucester before it splintered, allowing Langdon to dive over.

Missing the impetus of injured fly-half Fin Smith , Saints continued to struggle in attack after the restart with another promising opportunity snuffed out by a Joseph interception.

With both defences on top, the game needed a moment of real quality and eventually received it from Belleau.

With the Gloucester defence narrow, the fly-half played a perfect looped pass to Hendy who dived over in the corner to give Saints the lead.

Hutchinson then added a bonus point fourth, the replacement centre exploiting Gloucester's press defence with a quick step to force his way over the line.

Gloucester continued pressing until the end but were unable to breach the Saints defence, recording only their second loss of the season.

'We were alive to opportunities' - reaction

Northampton Saints head coach Sam Vesty told BBC Radio Northampton:

"[It was] a really satisfying win, a real contest of attack and defence, where both defences were tested but stood up.

"We started doing a lot of things better with 10 minutes to go in the first half. We moved off the ball better, created opportunities and we got that try just before half-time which is always a good time to score.

"In a game where defences are strong, you have to be pretty ruthless and we were alive to the opportunities, which was good to see."

"He felt something in his hamstring, we can't know more than that. It may not be too bad but then nobody who pulls their hamstring thinks it's bad."

Gloucester head coach George Skivington told BBC Radio Gloucestershire:

"We came out of the blocks well, attacked the game, but we just weren't accurate enough especially at the back-end of the first-half.

"We had some real opportunities and could've come in 14 or even 21 nil up, but we gave away a couple of penalties, they scored too easily and suddenly it was 14 all.

"We didn't get the launches and the ball through the hands the way we wanted to. The boys stayed in the fight, kept trying, but a lot of our play was scrappy balls, picking balls off the floor and Saints took their opportunities really well.

"There will be some good learnings here."

Northampton: Pater; Sleightholme, Freeman, Dingwall (c), Hendy; Belleau, Mitchell; Iyogun, Langdon, Kundiona; Coles, Prowse, Kemeny, Pearson, Chick.

Replacements: Smith, Fischetti, Neculai, Van Der Mescht, Lockett, Pollock, Weimann, Hutchinson.

Gloucester: Barton; Joseph, Llewellyn, S Atkinson (c), W Knight; C Atkinson, Englefield; Rapava Ruskin, Blake, Fasogbon; Kleyn, Clark, Thomas, Gwynne, Clement.

Replacements: Lake, Bleuler, C Knight, Trenholm, Morgan, Ludlow, Robson, Redshaw.

images.caption: Image caption, Max Llewellyn scored the first of Gloucester's tries but the Cherry and Whites failed to score in the second half

articles.title: Ospreys 0-26 Cardiff: Two-try Tom Bowen provides URC derby success
articles.summary: Cardiff lift themselves back into the top half of the United Rugby Championship (URC) by defeating Ospreys 26-0 in a scrappy Welsh derby at St Helen's.
articles.body:
Tries: Bowen 2, Adams, Howe Cons: Evans 2, Sheedy

Cardiff lifted themselves back into the top half of the United Rugby Championship (URC) by defeating Ospreys 26-0 in a scrappy Welsh derby at St Helen's.

Two tries from wing Tom Bowen and further scores from Josh Adams and hooker Tom Howe sealed the away bonus-point success against a lacklustre home side in Swansea.

Ospreys previously failed to score in a 23-0 defeat against Munster in October 2024.

Cardiff centre Steffan Emanuel was a creative influence and should prove an option for Wales if they pick up any midfield injuries next month.

His contribution was a shining light in a dour derby played in front of a 5,592 sell-out, with the occasion marred by the continued whistle of referee Ben Breakspear.

It was the second game at the revamped St Helen's ground after the opening Ospreys victory against Dragons .

The URC takes a break for five weeks, with the Nations Championship staged in November. Cardiff finish the first league block in seventh and Ospreys in ninth.

While there has been renewed talk of an Anglo-Welsh league this week , the URC match schedulers should reflect on their fixture choices with a significant Welsh derby staged a week before an international campaign and shorn of the Wales stars.

Adams was the only Welsh region-based member of Steve Tandy's squad to be sent out for game time prior to the Nations Championship.

Cardiff were without their six other Wales squad members, including Rhys Barratt, hooker Liam Belcher, lock Teddy Williams and back-row trio Alex Mann, James Botham and Taine Basham.

Full-back Tom Rogers, fly-half Dan Edwards, scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams and loose-head prop Gareth Thomas sat out for Ospreys.

With fly-half Lawson Creighton a late withdrawal because of a groin injury, Harri Wilde, who was on loan at Ospreys from Cardiff, started against his parent club. Wilde formed a third-choice half-back partnership with Luke Davies.

Cardiff enjoyed all the early pressure and were rewarded with a walk in for wing Bowen.

Ospreys appeared to have responded when prop Steffan Thomas was driven over, but after the try was initially given, the television match official (TMO) disallowed it after it was deemed that Cardiff scrum-half Johan Mulder had prevented the grounding.

Cardiff weathered the Ospreys attack and produced a well-worked scrum set-piece move which saw Bowen sprint over for his second.

Emanuel almost created a third try with a fine break and kick, but the Ospreys defence scrambled back and held firm.

Following a Dan Thomas turnover penalty, Emanuel turned creator with his deft kick being latched onto by Adams.

Ospreys suffered another blow when flanker Ross Moriarty suffered a nasty head injury and was replaced by Morgan Morse as dominant Cardiff took a deserved 19-0 half-time lead.

Ospreys started the second half with scrummaging superiority, with Cardiff replacing props Keiron Assiratti and Danny Southworth with international duo Scott Sio and Javan Sebastian.

Adams received treatment for a knee injury but was able to continue before Ospreys co-captain Sam Parry was held up over the Cardiff line.

Cardiff were warned for persistent penalties, and the frustrations of the Ospreys players with how the officials were interpreting the breakdown could be heard.

Cardiff repelled the Ospreys' defence with teenage replacement hooker Howe winning a crucial turnover penalty as the visitors‘ dynamic defence kept Ospreys at bay.

Howe gained his reward as Cardiff demonstrated a clinical approach, with the 18-year-old securing the bonus-point try after being driven over.

It was the only score as Emanuel denied Keelan Giles in the dying seconds with a wonderful covering tackle to complete the impressive victory.

The woeful second half was short on quality, but Cardiff's players, coaches and supporters will not care as they secured maximum points against an Ospreys side that looked devoid of attacking ideas.

Ospreys: Hopkins; Morgan, Watkin (co-capt), K Williams, Giles; Wilde, L Davies; S Thomas, Parry (co-capt), Botha, Ratti, Smith, Wright, Moriarty, M Morris.

Replacements: Daniel, C Jones, Warren, Sutton, Morse, H Williams, S Jac Jones, Boshoff.

Cardiff: Young; Adams, Malan, Emanuel, Bowen; J Evans, Mulder; Southworth, Hughes, Assiratti, McNally (capt), Thornton, Paea, Thomas, Lawrence.

Replacements: Howe, Sio, Sebastian, Manz, de la Rua, A Davies, Sheedy, Darwin-Lewis.

Assistant referees: Carwyn Sion & Marc Caudle (Wales)

images.caption: Image caption, Tom Bowen made 15 appearances for Cardiff in the 2025-26 season and scored eight tries

articles.title: Joe Hawkins: Wales centre determined to make World Cup after missing 2023 tournament
articles.summary: Wales centre Joe Hawkins says missing the previous World Cup has made him more determined to make the next global tournament in Australia in 12 months.
articles.body:
Wales centre Joe Hawkins says missing the previous World Cup has made him more determined to make the next global tournament in Australia in 12 months.

Following his move from Ospreys to Exeter in 2023, Hawkins was deemed ineligible to play for Wales by Welsh rugby's Professional Rugby Board (PRB) because of the 25-cap rule.

The rule says players who have fewer than 25 caps are unavailable to play for Wales if they are not involved with a Welsh club.

This ruled him out of the 2023 World Cup in France but Hawkins has since returned to the national side after signing for Scarlets.

"I have no regrets," said 24-year-old Hawkins.

"It would have been nice to have a World Cup under my belt already, but that just makes me even more excited for potentially what's ahead over the next year.

"I loved my couple of years in Exeter with the life experience and playing in the Prem, where you can see a lot of the boys are thriving in now."

Wales have a minimum of 12 matches before the World Cup, starting with the Nations Championship opener against Japan in Cardiff next Saturday.

"It's always in the back of your mind, knowing you're going into a World Cup year," said Hawkins.

"You can probably see from performances from other boys in all positions in the squads that in a World Cup year, the intensity probably rises at the clubs.

"Boys are playing for positions and knowing that's the carrot at the end of the year.

"But if you're not taking care of the here and now you're not going to get that far."

Wales wing Mee signs new Scarlets contract

Davies backs Page to make Wales debut soon

Where are Wales internationals really made?

Hawkins, 24, and Scarlets partner Eddie James have developed as Wales' first-choice centre pairing during the past 12 months.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy has selected five different starting midfield partnerships in 13 games since taking charge in September 2025.

Hawkins and James are the most prolific pair, having been together for seven games which include victory in an uncapped match against Barbarians.

Tandy did go back to Ben Thomas and Max Llewellyn for the 43-0 defeat by South Africa in July, but the Scarlets pair have been the preferred option.

"Eddie and I have a good relationship on and off the field," said Hawkins.

"That is starting to grow on the pitch with the more opportunities we get together."

The make-up of the Wales midfield has caused debate with Tandy and attack coach Matt Sherratt wanting a creative ball-playing inside centre like Hawkins or Thomas.

This leaves James as the physical presence at outside centre with Tandy stating he sees the Carmarthen-born 24-year-old's long-term future as a Test 13.

Many observers believe James should be considered as a 12 but Wales are determined to keep their creative options open.

With Thomas missing because of a calf injury, Hawkins appears to be competing for the Wales' 12 jersey with uncapped Dragons centre Aneurin Owen, although Llewellyn has also featured at inside centre for Gloucester this season.

"The ball-playing stuff is stuff I enjoy doing but you still need to go forward as well and I feel like I can also produce that side of it," said Hawkins.

"Matt [Sherratt] likes you always in and around that first receiver position so you are always in those decision-making roles.

"You've got to be comfortable on the ball and making decisions at high speed.

"But there's not always going to be opportunities to ball play, so you've got to try and have a bit of a rounded game."

Hawkins has also been employed as an outside-half by Scarlets but he sees his future at 12.

"It gives me a lot more respect for the 10s, having been in there, with all the work they do," he added.

"It probably helps me when I play centre from being a 10, I know what they need from me a little bit more, so the information and communication I'm feeding helps the whole team."

images.caption: Image caption, Joe Hawkins is a former Wales Under-20s international
Image caption, Joe Hawkins (right) has played 13 internationals for Wales

articles.title: Women's Rugby League World Cup: Australia hit debutants Wales for record score
articles.summary: Wales women concede 21 tries in Sydney as defending Rugby League World Cup champions Australia rewrite the international record books.
articles.body:
Tries: Kernick, Chapman 6, Church 2, Southwell, Sergis 4, Apps, Paki, Joseph 2, Upton 2, Nizza Goals: Southwell 20

Rampant Australia racked up the biggest score in international history as they hammered Wales in a Rugby League World Cup mismatch.

The Jillaroos, hunting a fourth successive title, ran in 21 tries in a predictably lopsided contest in Sydney.

The half-time score of 60-0 was the biggest of any World Cup match - men's or women's - and the Australians kept their foot down to win 124-6.

Wing Jaime Chapman's sixth try in the last minute ensured they beat Denmark men's biggest international score of 122-8 against Sweden in 2012.

The 118-point victory margin is the largest in any women's match, although France men retain their record win set in 2003 with a 120-0 rout of Serbia.

Yet there were wild Wales celebrations when, at 100-0 down, they became the first side to score against the Jillaroos in the tournament through Paige Travis.

Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand

Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

The Jillaroos are three-time back-to-back champions, while Wales were taking part in the tournament for the first time having only played their first Test in 2021.

It was just their 16th fixture - and a first against Australia - with Tom Brindle's side having already been beaten 70-6 by England and 76-0 by Samoa at the World Cup.

Full of NRLW talent, Australia showed a killer instinct and an intensity that Wales were exposed to for the first time.

It all came after Wales, whose captain Bethan Dainton was the tournament's top tackler by a distance in the first two rounds with 77, rose to the occasion with a strong start.

But Australia struck in the sixth minute through lock Olivia Kernick following prop Makenzie Weale's terrific offload out the back, and the Jillaroos then clicked into gear.

Long-striding, hard-fending Chapman scored a double down the left and fellow wing Abbi Church powered through weak tackles on the right.

Wales were unable to string together good moments and a fifth try came through Jesse Southwell from failure to claim a regulation high ball just seconds after Jade Mullen had put in a huge tackle.

Australia were ruthless and the scores kept coming through centre Jessica Sergis, second row Kezie Apps and Chapman for a first-half hat-trick.

Sergis brought up the half-century with a weaving run and was followed over by second row Sariah Paki.

The stats told the story - Australia had 84% of possession in the first half and completed 21 of 22 sets, with almost 13 minutes of possession to two minutes and 29 seconds.

It took just over a minute for Keilee Joseph to get the scoreboard ticking after the restart and the scores kept coming from Sergis, Chapman, Joseph again and Church.

The Jillaroos beat their 92-0 record, set against France in the 2022 World Cup, when Southwell converted Sergis' fourth try, hitting three figures when the extras were added to star full-back Tamika Upton's breakaway.

Wales' moment came when Travis, scorer of their historic try against England, won the race to Tayla Preston's kick through.

It was only a brief change of pattern with Keeley Nizza, Chapman twice and Upton going over to complete the destruction.

"We just wanted to create a legacy back home for young girls coming through, and I think we did that. The scorelines haven't been in our favour but no one gave up and I am so proud of the girls."

images.caption: Image caption, Jessica Sergis scored one of Australia's 10 converted tries in the first half against Wales

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: England's elimination confirmed after Tonga beat Samoa in the final group match
articles.summary: England suffer historic group-stage exit at the Rugby League World Cup with Tonga unable to defeat Samoa by more than 46 points; Tonga will play New Zealand in the last four, while Samoa will face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final
articles.body:
England sealed a 34-12 victory against Papua New Guinea on Friday but needed to win by a big margin to give themselves a chance of leapfrogging Samoa in Pool B and C and advancing to the semi-finals on points difference.

Brian McDermott's side's hopes rested on Tonga to win by more than 46 points to reach the last four for the seventh successive tournament.

Instead they are on the plane home from Australasia despite winning two of their three matches.

The 30-12 defeat by Tonga in the opening match proved costly, with an 82-0 win over France leaving England with 68 points to make up on Samoa.

They failed to make significant enough inroads in the 32-10 win over Papua New Guinea.

English hopes briefly flickered when Tonga led 8-0, Robert Toia scoring the opening try after a near 50-metre sprint.

With Isaiya Katoa converting and then kicking a penalty, England just needed Tonga to score another 39 unanswered points to stay in the tournament.

However, Brian To'o's try hauled Samoa back to 8-4 down at half-time.

Jojo Fifita put Tonga 14-4 ahead before To'o, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and Ronald Volkman edged Samoa into a two-point lead, only for Addin Fonua-Blake to win it for Tonga.

Tonga will play New Zealand in the last four, while Samoa will face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.

Is the Rugby League World Cup format flawed?

The new tournament structure, which has been downsized from 16 teams to 10, came after Australia stepped in as hosts following France's withdrawal in 2023 for financial reasons.

It has effectively meant that each group game in Pool B and C has carried more jeopardy than before.

The tournament has two pools, one featuring four teams - Australia, New Zealand, Cook Islands and Fiji - and the other featuring six teams.

England were drawn in the second group, Pool B and C, alongside Tonga, Samoa, Papua New Guinea, Lebanon and France.

The top two teams from each group qualify for the knockout rounds, and in the event of a tie, teams are judged on their head-to-head record before points difference.

McDermott's side were beaten in their first match against Tonga which put their hopes of qualifying in the balance, despite later thrashing France by 82 points in round two.

Sky Sports' Jon Wilkin said: "Australia have done a great job to organise a tournament in such a short space of time, but it was fundamentally flawed, unfair in the extreme to the start.

"The actual competition structure is just diabolical. England were dealt an incredibly difficult task, because they essentially played their quarter-final in week one."

"England knew after their loss against Tonga that it was all going to be about points difference, and [qualifying] was going to be incredibly difficult," Wilkin said. "I think the structure and the setup of the competition was done in short notice.

"I think the International Rugby League, who set up this tournament, have done an incredible job to get it on and actually and get in a position where we can have the tournament.

"So, I commend them for that, but I just think the tournament structure is laughable. Like, no quarter-finals? There's a number of ways you could have manufactured or engineered a quarter-finals situation.

"England should be in the quarter-finals, of the World Cup. They had a disappointing 30-40 minutes against Tonga, and they're out."

RFL invites England legends to discuss national sides' international future

Some of the greatest players in England's modern history will convene to help map out a future for the national game, including further analysis of the pyramid, from grassroots and pathways to the player pool for the international stage.

After the disappointment of seeing England miss out on the World Cup semi-finals across both the men's and women's competition, recently-appointed RFL Chief Executive Ian Nolan has decided to call upon the knowledge of a raft of stellar quality to form an in-depth discussion on national performance.

Former Great Britain captain Paul Sculthorpe MBE and iconic forward Adrian Morley are among the names of those who will now get together to look at what extra can be done to help make the England teams a genuine force.

They will be joined by Gareth Ellis, who played in the last Men's side from these shores to defeat world champions Australia in 2006 and works as a current assistant coach with York Knights, plus recently retired St Helens and England captain Jodie Cunningham who will bring valuable perspectives for the Women's and Girls' game.

images.caption: Image: Robert Toia of Tonga celebrates scoring against Samoa at CommBank Stadium
Image: England's defeat by Tonga in the opening match proved costly
Image: Adrian Morley will be among the names to help map out a future for the national game

articles.title: England turn to past greats after crashing out of Rugby League World Cup
articles.summary: Both England’s men and women failed to make the semi-finals in disappointing tournaments
articles.body:
England have turned to a panel of past greats in a bid to address the shortcomings that led to both their men and women crashing out of the Rugby League World Cup in the pool stages.

Brian McDermott 's men failed to make the semi-finals for the first time in competition history, with their exit confirmed by Tonga's narrow win over Samoa in Sydney on Sunday.

England had been beaten by Tonga in their opening game and though they bounced back to thrash France, a clunky performance against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong in their final pool game all but ended their chances.

For the women, meanwhile, the gap to Australia was underscored in a 78-0 humbling, while Samoa were convincing 24-6 winners on Friday.

The twin tournament exits come at a time of tumult for the sport , with negotiations continuing over a proposed deal that will see Australia's National Rugby League ( NRL ) invest in Super League .

That agreement is expected to come under the proviso that the London Broncos are elevated into a 15-team top tier. Super League currently has no title sponsor, television deal or fixtures for next season.

Recently-appointed Rugby Football League (RFL) chief executive Ian Nolan has in the meantime formed a panel of ex-internationals to consult on the best route forward for the sport in England, noting underperformance stretching back "half a century".

Former Great Britain captain Paul Sculthorpe will be joined by Jodie Cunningham, who concluded her playing career after leading England at the World Cup, as well as Adrian Morley and Gareth Ellis – both part of the last British team to beat the Kangaroos in 2006. Additional members are yet to be confirmed.

The panel's analysis remit will be wide-reaching. England's chances in Australia were not helped by a convoluted format and demanding travel itinerary, while executives have faced criticism after the BBC did not take up rights to the competition, which was instead shown on Premier Sports in the United Kingdom.

"In this World Cup, Brian McDermott and his Men's squad have delivered two wins from their three games and shown signs of genuine quality," Nolan, who took up his role four weeks ago, said.

"The 82-0 win over France was as emphatic as anyone could have hoped for and the opening 20 minutes against Papua New Guinea on Friday was similarly impressive.

"Sadly, we couldn't quite maintain that level throughout, but we still emerged with two wins and were unfortunate, in many ways, to not prosper versus Tonga in our opener.

"This analysis of our national game will be all encompassing, including how we can influence media rights, balancing reach and revenue, and attracting new audiences.

"But on the pitch, we must look at why we have consistently struggled to make our mark on the world stage for more than half a century; this isn't just a recent problem. "

McDermott was appointed in April but did not have any pre-tournament fixtures with which to work with the squad, and remains based in the NRL as an assistant coach with the Gold Coast Titans.

The semi-finals will be made up of four sides with a heavy NRL influence, with Tonga taking on New Zealand and Samoa facing Australia for a place in the showpiece decider.

images.caption: Jodie Cunningham will be part of the panel formed (PA Archive)

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: How England plan to avoid repeat of early exit
articles.summary: After England exit the Men's and Women's Rugby League World Cups at the group stage, the RFL announces plans designed to prevent a repeat.
articles.body:
The time for excuses is over - and those in charge of English rugby league know it.

There were mitigating circumstances behind England's early departures from the Men's and Women's Rugby League World Cups.

But there is also an acknowledgement within the Rugby Football League that, for both the men and the women, a group-stage exit is just not good enough.

Within minutes of the men's exit being confirmed on Sunday morning as Tonga defeated Samoa 20-18 in an epic, the RFL had announced a plan to map out the future of the English game.

Former Great Britain men's captain Paul Sculthorpe, retiring England women's skipper Jodie Cunningham and international great Adrian Morley will be among those helping to put together that plan.

The RFL has promised more names will be confirmed on the panel in the coming days - to build on work started earlier in the year under a scheme it is calling One Game, One England.

Its aims - to build a system that develops players from grassroots and academy level who will ultimately be good enough for the international stage - chime with the recent words of Brian McDermott, head coach of England's men's team.

McDermott has spoken more than once during this World Cup campaign about the need to strengthen the structures of the English domestic game in order to give the national team a fighting chance.

And while England were not helped by their travel schedule, or a group format that effectively meant they were facing elimination from the moment they lost their opening match to Tonga, or injuries that robbed them of key players, they will not pretend that all is fine.

Set up to fail? Where England's World Cup campaign went wrong

McDermott calls for Super League to accept NRL investment

England's travel schedule like Steve Martin comedy - McDermott

Ian Nolan, the RFL's new chief executive, has made clear that he recognises that.

"There are plenty of mitigating reasons why we failed to reach the knockout stages, many of which were out of our control, such as travel itineraries and format of the competition, but we can't use these as excuses," Nolan said.

"Likewise, we were also criticised for what happened with the TV rights and the tournament going behind a paywall [on Premier Sports]. We had no control over who the rights were sold to. However, television is an important element of capturing the imagination of the next generation.

"This analysis of our national game will be all-encompassing, including how we can influence media rights, balancing reach and revenue, and attracting new audiences.

"But on the pitch, we must look at why we have consistently struggled to make our mark on the world stage for more than half a century; this isn't just a recent problem."

England's women have not been helped by the fact they are playing in a domestic competition - the Women's Super League - that is effectively amateur, while being asked to compete at a World Cup against professionals from Australia's NRL Women's Premiership.

But they do have a development programme in place - the Diploma in Sporting Excellence (DiSE) is designed to bring through young female players, in years 12 and 13 of the education system, who have the potential to play at the elite level.

"Grassroots investment in our women and girls' game only started a few years ago," Nolan said. "We've started that journey.

"Stuart Barrow took a very young side to this World Cup, with 11 graduates from our DiSE programme. We're very much building for the next World Cups – the average age of our squad was just 21 years old - but the groundwork is starting to pay off."

Twelve months on, another disappointment

England's exit from the Men's Rugby League World Cup was confirmed on Sunday, exactly 12 months to the day after their Rugby League Ashes challenge officially ended.

On 1 November last year, Australia won 14-4 in the second Test at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium to secure a series victory.

That defeat, and the one that followed in the third Test at Headingley seven days later, set in motion the chain of events that led to Shaun Wane's departure as head coach. He left in January and McDermott arrived in April.

McDermott - with no mid-season international or warm-up matches to fine-tune a style of play - has produced improvements.

England were good in patches against Tonga, were as ruthless as they needed to be against France, and were doing everything required of them for the opening 20 minutes against Papua New Guinea before losing their way completely.

McDermott wants to stay on for the 2030 World Cup and, given the right preparation time, could well bring further progress.

He is, however, fighting with one hand tied behind his back.

Australia's NRL is king in the rugby league universe: the seven-year, A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television contract it signed in July is evidence of that. The three-match State of Origin series, staged in June and July, dominates the calendar at the point Europe might try to squeeze in an international window.

It means that if England want to play the southern hemisphere sides - as they must in order to keep improving - they can only do so in October and November, and even then must work around the southern hemisphere's Pacific Championships.

That makes it even more important that English domestic rugby league finds a way to bridge the quality gap between itself and the Australian game - to ensure Super League players are facing the best week in, week out.

The NRL's ongoing negotiations to invest in Super League may help. Peter V'landys - chairman of the Australian Rugby League Commission, the NRL's parent body - remains keen to do a deal despite a struggle to reach agreement.

"I think there's some dominoes could start falling our way if the NRL invests and we accept their investment," McDermott said just under two weeks ago.

But as he has also pointed out, the problems in English rugby league are too deep to be solved quickly with financial investment.

"New South Wales clubs have got about six teams [from youth level up to the senior side]," McDermott said last month. "And every one of those teams have got a six [stand-off], a seven [scrum-half] and a nine [hooker] and a one [full-back]. And they all play consistently.

"Super League clubs... I don't think they could populate three teams underneath them with a genuine six, seven, nine and one [the spine of the team].

"And this is not a new opinion, this has been going on for a long time.

"It's nothing to do with professionalism. It's nothing to do with commitment. It's nothing to do with good quality coaching or commitment from players. It's just the size of the competitions."

What is clear is whatever the future for English rugby league, there are no quick fixes, even with the One Game, One England panel in place.

As Nolan puts it: "The panel will help us form some big decisions and changes. Those decisions might need the support of the entire game, and progress won't be achieved overnight. These will be changes that pay off in four, eight, 10 years' time."

images.caption: Image caption, England's men won two of their three group games and finished with a points difference of +86, but it was not enough

articles.title: Rating the Welsh club's start to 2026-27 season in URC and Europe
articles.summary: Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets finish their first blocks of the season in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship.
articles.body:
Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets are ready for November breaks after completing the first block of the domestic 2026-27 season.

The United Rugby Championship (URC) is on hold while four rounds are played in the Nations Championship.

Cardiff and Dragons are setting the pace on 14 points, with the seventh-placed Blue and Blacks edging in front on win count.

Ospreys and Scarlets have work to do but have got their tough double-headers in South Africa out of the way.

There has also been a round of European rugby, with the Blue and Blacks losing in the Champions Cup and the other three winning in the second-tier Challenge Cup.

How will the Welsh quartet reflect on a first chunk of the season that featured a derby in every league round?

Centre Hawkins determined to make World Cup

The Prem talents hunting Wales breakthroughs

Cardiff were Wales' standard bearers in 2025-26 when they finished sixth and qualified for the play-offs for the first time.

The Blue and Blacks have been a mixed bag, but got a crucial 26-0 win against Ospreys in Swansea to finish.

"We have been fighting for a performance like that all of this first block," said lock Josh McNally.

"The group is in a really good place and everybody is aligned with what we want to do. When it clicks we can put in a performance like that."

It was a strong response to a rare poor display at the Arms Park against Sharks, which had the mitigation of a five-day turnaround from a defeat by English champions Northampton.

Taine Basham has been a stand-out performer at number eight to earn a Wales recall, while hugely promising 20-year-old centre Steffan Emanuel capped a strong first block with a man-of-the-match performance at Ospreys.

"The break is at a decent time which will allow us to work on stuff we haven't been so great at, then go again for a massive run of games," said head coach Corniel van Zyl.

Cardiff will mix their URC play-off bid with facing top-tier European opposition in the next block.

They have a mouth-watering home Champions Cup fixture against Bath in December, then games against Stade Francais and Montpellier.

Northampton 28-12 Cardiff (Champions Cup)

Dragons head coach Filo Tiatia declared that he was content with their first block after his side avoided a slip against winless Zebre.

"I am happy with where we are, but we have a lot of work to do," he said.

"The next block is so important and it's five weeks before we hit Edinburgh, then there are nine games to Munster at the end of January.

"We need everyone fit, fresh and ready to scrap for the club."

The November break is timely for Dragons, whose squad was creaking for Zebre.

They were without 18 players due to five Wales calls and injuries, while several players were bruised and battered.

That comes after an encouraging first block that featured three wins, a draw and a missed opportunity at Benetton but two disappointments against Ospreys.

Dragons got their Challenge Cup campaign off to a winning start against Perpignan and have 14 points in the URC.

That is half of last year's total, although they are yet to play a side that made the 2026 play-offs and none of those they have faced are in the current top half.

The driving line-out has been a weapon, Tonga wing Anzelo Tuitavuki has scored tries in five successive games and the attack looks more threatening.

"We got some stats through at the end of last season around where we sat in terms of our attacking game," said coach Matt O'Brien.

"We were pretty good at our launch stuff - our line-out and scrum attack - but our unstructured game needed a bit of work.

"We focused heavily on that and have had some good improvements, with our offloading one of those areas."

Dragons will hope their Wales contingent of Aneurin Owen, Che Hope, Dillon Lewis, Ben Carter and Seb Davies, Argentina prop Rodrigo Martinez and Tongans Tuitavuki, Fetuli Paea and Fine Inisi come back unscathed.

Dragons trio continuing Gwent's Tongan tradition

It looked set to be an encouraging first block for Ospreys until they were thumped by Cardiff and Mark Jones’ side will spend the next month reflecting ruefully on such a humbling home defeat in a local derby.

Ospreys racked up the air miles while major work was done to get St Helen's ready for their Swansea homecoming.

Jones has given 35 players starts, rotating due to a schedule that saw them play in Durban, Johannesburg, Newport and Tbilisi.

Former Australia captain Liam Wright has been a positive as he attempts to put several years of injury misfortune behind him.

The blind-side flanker has started all five URC games and impressed with his work rate, line-out skills and leadership.

A rib injury suffered on debut means that former Wallabies wing Marika Koroibete has not been able to make the same impact in the first block.

A double of Dragons, with a maximum 10 points, ensures that is remains a solid start, despite being nilled by Cardiff.

Jones said: "We are still a big work in progress. There is lots to do in our game, including the consistency with which we do things.

"It was a nice little reminder of the level that you need to get to in the URC if you want to get victories."

Three of Ospreys' next four fixtures are at St Helen's - with champions Leinster next up on Friday, 4 December.

"We've got to ponder on the Cardiff defeat and get the work in, because you can't expect results for work you don't do," said Jones.

Black Lion 14-39 Ospreys (Challenge Cup)

Ospreylia: How Welsh club turned to a land down under

Scarlets, like Ospreys, have got their South Africa trip out of the way and took encouragement from their games at Stormers and Bulls despite two losses.

Nigel Davies' side made another slow start to the campaign with derby defeats against Cardiff and Scarlets.

They appear to have rediscovered their swagger in recent weeks with an expansive approach, while number eight Fletcher Anderson has shown his value on his return from injury.

The New Zealander has added big ball-carrying threat to go along with the wide threat that has earned four try bonuses in five URC games, and a Wales call-up for livewire wing Macs Page.

However, Zebre are the only team to have conceded more than their 29 tries.

New defence coach Eamon O'Carroll completed the Super League season with St Helens and has plenty of work to do.

"In terms of the style of rugby, how we want to go about our business and the behaviours from players on the field, we're seeing a lot of real positives and we're tracking in the right direction," said director of rugby Davies before the defeat by Bulls.

"They've grown as a group. We weren't really firing on all cylinders in the first couple of games, we've started to find our feet a little bit."

Scarlets return to action with a home fixture against Connacht before three away games on the bounce, Sharks in the Challenge Cup, Munster and Ospreys.

Scarlets 47-14 Newcastle (Challenge Cup)

articles.title: Steve Borthwick: England must quickly adjust from Prem to Test rugby for Nations Championship
articles.summary: England will name squad on Monday for Nations Championship Tests against Australia (Nov 8), Japan (Nov 14) and New Zealand (Nov 21) this November; head coach Steve Borthwick admits his squad will need to adjust from Prem Rugby to Test Rugby far quicker in order to succeed this Autumn
articles.body:
Australia's visit to Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Sunday marks the start of the second phase of the inaugural Nations Championship. Borthwick knows England will need to raise their standards at the breakdown and in defence if they are to compete successfully.

While the Prem's focus on attack has created some thrilling spectacles, it is inadequate preparation for the battles to come against the Wallabies, Japan and New Zealand.

The only round of Champions Cup action so far this season exposed English clubs to a different level of competition in defence and at the breakdown, as they managed just one win from eight matches.

Referee Christophe Ridley provided assistance in training at last week's camp and also gave presentations to the squad in a bid to accelerate their readiness to take on Australia.

"The contact area in the Prem is different to Test rugby," Borthwick said. "That was exemplified in Europe where the English clubs lost more ball and won back less ball at the breakdown than any other nation.

"The other area is the emphasis and importance placed upon defence. We need to ensure that we make it very, very difficult for the opposition to score.

"One of the challenges is that we are refereed domestically by English referees when internationally, quite clearly, we will never have the English referees, so you need to get used to other interpretations.

"Having that European round pleased me because clearly players needed to be able to adjust. The best players are smart and the best players adjust.

"And I think it's pretty obvious that over the last six to eight months, we haven't adjusted and dealt with moments in the way we want to."

England have amassed 15 yellow cards in their eight Tests so far this year, including four in their most recent outing against Argentina in July. Borthwick believes going on the attack provides the solution to the indiscipline.

"Frankly, we spend too much time defending," he said. "The way the interpretations are right now, as soon as you spend time defending there is likely to be a decision that goes against you.

"There has been an exponential increase in cards given - and not just by us. The vast majority of them are given when defending in your own 22."

England are facing mounting problems at half-back ahead of Monday's squad announcement after Alex Mitchell followed Fin Smith and Archie McParland into the treatment room.

Mitchell has joined his Northampton team-mates in becoming a doubt against Australia after sustaining a hamstring injury in Saturday's 28-14 victory over Gloucester.

articles.title: Nations Championship: What can Wales expect in November?
articles.summary: BBC Sport Wales provides a recap of what has happened so far in the inaugural Nations Championship and what will occur during the next month?
articles.body:
Wales will start their international season next weekend when they return to the Nations Championship.

Steve Tandy's side face four games as they host Japan, New Zealand and Australia in Cardiff, before a final play-off match at the Allianz Stadium completes the November schedule.

The autumn games begin the road to the 2027 World Cup in Australia in a year's time.

BBC Sport Wales provides a recap of what has happened so far in the inaugural running of the global tournament and looks at what lies in wait over the next month.

The Nations Championship pits the northern hemisphere teams who compete in the Six Nations - England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy - against southern hemisphere giants South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina, plus invited sides Fiji and Japan.

All teams play each of the six nations in the opposing hemisphere once, with three rounds of fixtures having already been staged in July and now another three in November.

Their results will rank the teams within their own hemisphere, from one to six, before a final play-off weekend at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

Where are Wales internationals really made?

Wales counting down the year until World Cup

How have Wales fared so far and who do they play next?

Wales will resume the Nations Championship in fifth place in the northern hemisphere standings after a mixed July campaign.

It started with an encouraging six-try victory against Fiji at the Cardiff City Stadium, which was considered a home venue for the Pacific Islanders side.

But Wales faltered during a demanding travelling schedule as they were outclassed by Argentina in San Juan and thrashed by South Africa in Durban.

Now they face a trio of home games in Cardiff with the opening match staged against Eddie Jones' Japan side, who also sit fifth in their table, with the two teams potentially meeting twice this November.

The tests will become harder when Dave Rennie brings his New Zealand side to Cardiff on 14 November, before the Wallabies arrive seven days later.

Saturday, 11 July: Argentina 35-21 Wales

Saturday, 18 July: South Africa 43-0 Wales

Saturday, 7 November: Wales v Japan, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 16:40 GMT

Saturday, 14 November: Wales v New Zealand, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 14:10 GMT

Saturday, 21 November: Wales v Australia, Principality Stadium, Cardiff, 20:10 GMT.

Uncapped Dragons duo Aneurin Owen and Che Hope, and Cardiff prop Rhys Barrett were named in a 39-strong group for the November Tests, with hooker Dewi Lake again handed the captaincy.

Head coach Tandy called up Dragons lock Seb Davies and Cardiff number eight Taine Basham for the first time since he took charge of the national side.

Dragons wing Rio Dyer initially earned a recall, but was ruled out because of a hamstring injury and replaced by uncapped Scarlets back Macs Page.

Leicester flanker Tommy Reffell and scrum-half Kieran Hardy were among the notable absentees because of injury, while veteran number eight Taulupe Faletau is also absent.

Fifteen of the players are based outside of Wales with 14 plying their club trade in England and Montpellier lock Adam Beard based in France.

Forwards: Rhys Barratt, Rhys Carre, Nicky Smith, Gareth Thomas, Dewi Lake (capt), Liam Belcher, Ryan Elias, Tomas Francis, Archie Griffin, Dillon Lewis, Adam Beard, Ben Carter, Seb Davies, Dafydd Jenkins, Teddy Williams, Taine Basham, James Botham, Kane James, Alex Mann, Jac Morgan, Taine Plumtree, Aaron Wainwright.

Backs: Che Hope, Reuben Morgan-Williams, Tomos Williams, Sam Costelow, Dan Edwards, Joe Hawkins, Louie Hennessey, Eddie James, Max Llewellyn, Aneurin Owen, Josh Adams, Macs Page, Gabriel Hamer-Webb, Ellis Mee, Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Tom Rogers.

Early indications suggest there could empty seats at the Principality Stadium this autumn.

A look at the WRU website shows a significant amount of tickets still available for the three home matches.

The first test for Wales will be to match the 61,000 crowd that witnessed the dramatic 24-23 win against Japan 12 months ago.

Wales should expect a sellout against the All Blacks, especially given the favourable Saturday mid-afternoon kick-off time, although the late evening start against Australia a week later will provide its challenges.

The attendances will give an insight into whether the upheaval in Welsh rugby has affected interest in the game - or whether apathy is setting in.

The Wales players are again performing amid the backdrop of an uncertain domestic future with the WRU currently determined to stick to its policy of cutting Ospreys or Scarlets by 2028.

There will be an annual general meeting (AGM) held a day after Wales play Australia, while a rugby summit featuring the professional sides will be staged in December.

Ticket sales are important because they form more than 50% of the annual turnover of the WRU, who announced an £18m loss earlier this month.

'I'm no yes-man' - new WRU chair to review region cut

Prem eyes English expansion despite Welsh interest

WRU publishes data on why west Wales team will be cut

What happens at the final weekend at Twickenham?

On the final weekend in November, there is a three-day play-off event staged at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

The sixth-placed team in the northern hemisphere plays off against the equivalent in the southern hemisphere standings and so on, culminating in the two top-ranked sides taking each other on.

On Friday evening the sixth-placed and third-place finishers will face each other, while Saturday will see the fifth-place and second place matches.

The Sunday finale will see the fourth-placed sides compete before the winner of that final match between the top seeds crowned the inaugural Nations Championship winner.

There is also a parallel, Ryder-Cup style, hemisphere title.

The winner of each of the matches on the play-offs weekend will earn one point for their hemisphere, except for the contest between the two top-ranked teams which delivers two.

The first hemisphere to earn four points over the weekend will be crowned winners.

Sixth-place North v Sixth-place South (16:40 GMT)

Third-place North v Third-place South (20:10 GMT)

Fifth-place North v Fifth-place South (13:10 GMT)

Second-place North v Second-place South (16:40 GMT)

Fourth-place North v Fourth-place South (13:10 GMT)

First-place North v First-place South (16:40 GMT).

articles.title: Wales not finished product but all roads lead to 2029 World Cup
articles.summary: Head coach Sean Lynn says Wales are not the finished product but he has been encouraged by their WXV Global Series.
articles.body:
Head coach Sean Lynn admits Wales are far from the finished product but says he has been hugely encouraged by their WXV showings.

An eight-try mauling of South Africa in Cardiff and two Test wins out in Japan saw Wales finish World Rugby's new Global Series on a high.

Only a narrow two-point defeat by USA - a team ranked in the world's top six - prevented a clean sweep.

It marks quite the transformation for Lynn's side who had been on a nine-Test losing streak prior to the tournament and slumped to an all-time low world ranking of 13th.

"Twelve months ago we didn't win a game in the World Cup. We've worked so hard as a group of players and staff and we've come into this WXV with three out of four wins," said Lynn.

"Are we the finished product? No we're not, but we're seeing the bigger picture of that roadmap to the 2029 World Cup.

"There are areas that we need to be looking at and the players now need to go back to the PWR [Premiership Women's Rugby] and Celtic Challenge because we're still looking to move that dial.

"But I can't fault the effort from players and staff, it's been a really intense 11 weeks."

Lynn hails grit of 13-player Wales in Japan win

Wales complete Japan double to end WXV on a high

Wales' transformation began with a brutal pre-season during which Lynn secured the permanent services of assistant coaches Ashley Beck and Steve Salvin.

That, along with Tyrone Holmes' growing impact as defence coach and the introduction of strength and conditioning specialist Gareth Harris, gave Wales some much-needed stability.

"We've all been really specific about what we want to do. We've established a DNA and I'm really proud of all the hard work - physical and mental - that not just the players have put in, but also the staff," said Wales co-captain Kate Williams.

"It's competitive within the team and that's showing on the pitch as well against other teams."

Lynn has capped 12 new players during his 18 months in charge and in doing so has unearthed gems such as Seren Lockwood, Branwen Metcalfe, Freya Bell and Amy Williams.

"It's super important that we are always watching. Amy Williams for instance, what I saw of her at Cardiff Met and Brython Thunder, I really liked," he said.

"She's very brave, likes to get the ball in her hands and always wants to beat that first defender. Individuals like her and Freya Bell have been like ducks to water coming into the international arena and I believe there are more out there.

"The senior players are now having that competitive edge in the squad, and they know that the jersey is not theirs."

Lynn has shown he is not afraid to make big selection calls and has backed the youngsters all summer, with the first glimpse of his new-look side coming in the 34-17 victory over Barbarians.

While Lynn has enjoyed success with fresh blood, it remains unclear as to which is his preferred half-back partnership after experimenting with a few different combinations.

Kayleigh Powell went well at 10 alongside Lockwood against the Barbarians, but a hamstring injury ruled her out of the entire WXV campaign.

Keira Bevan - usually a scrum-half - played 10 against South Africa and Wales looked much better in attack when keeping ball in hand. But a head injury suffered by Lockwood meant we only saw about 30 minutes of that duo.

Lleucu George started at fly-half against USA and in the second Japan Test, with Wales reverting back to a kicking and territorial game.

Hopefully one pair will have a run of games during the 2027 Six Nations, allowing Wales to finally gain some continuity in such pivotal positions.

Not that they needed any extra incentives, but next year's historic women's British and Irish Lions tour would certainly have been in the back of players' minds heading into WXV.

Lions head coach Jo Yapp was at Cardiff Arms Park for Wales' demolition of the Springboks and also attended a training session.

And while the bulk of the team is still likely to be made up of England's World Cup-winning stars, there are some Wales players who have put their hand up.

Wales co-captain Alex Callender has been colossal. After missing the Six Nations through injury, the feisty flanker has exploded back onto the international scene, leading from the front with tackles and turnovers.

Prop Sisilia Tuipulotu is also back to her best. She is by far Wales' best ball carrier and has proven very difficult to stop having racked up four tries this autumn.

Bevan has showed Yapp a versatility in being able to play in both half-back positions, although her showing in the first Japan Test was a lot less convincing than against South Africa.

And then if you consider potential bolters, scrum-half Lockwood should be in the conversation. She has an international maturity well beyond her 20 years, is a huge threat at the breakdown and has a good eye for the try-line. She also looks equally as comfortable when moved out to the wing.

Quiz: Name the 12 players given Wales debuts by Lynn

Little Angel makes big impact on return to Japan

Wales have not won a Six Nations game since edging Italy in the final round of the 2024 championship.

And even though they open the 2027 edition against reigning champions England - instead of starting against Scotland as they have done for the past three years - they will surely take some confidence from their upturn in results.

"I know it's a long way away and a lot can happen, but for us going into the Six Nations and not actually starting against Scotland is exciting," said Lynn.

"We've got the Red Roses coming to the Principality, it's huge for players and staff."

Until then, Lynn and his staff will be keeping a watchful eye on the domestic leagues, which Callender says players head back to with "confidence".

Reflecting on the year as a whole, she said: "It's always a privilege to be able to wear the jersey and I'm just so proud of the girls.

"It's been a roller coaster, but it's all part of the sport isn't it?"

Let's hope the ride in 2027 will be just as enjoyable, with more ups than downs.

articles.title: England Rugby: Steve Borthwick and Henry Pollock backed by James Haskell ahead of Nations Championship fixtures
articles.summary: James Haskell believes Steve Borthwick is the right man to lead England at the 2027 Rugby World Cup and shares his excitement over rising star Henry Pollock ahead of November's Nations Championship fixtures against Australia, Japan and New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham
articles.body:
Borthwick oversaw England's worst-ever Six Nations campaign earlier this year, with four losses from their five matches, but despite growing pressure the RFU have publicly expressed their support for Borthwick through to the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia.

This month, England will face Australia, Japan and New Zealand ahead of Finals Weekend, which takes place November 27-28 at Twickenham.

Former England international Haskell, who earned 77 Test caps between 2007 and 2019, insists it is not the time to change the head coach.

"The RFU have got behind Steve Borthwick, and rightly so," Haskell told Sky Sports.

"I think he's the right man for the job."

Borthwick oversaw a 12-game unbeaten streak ahead of the 2026 Six Nations, and Haskell insists the change in performance is not as stark as the critics might suggest.

"It's never as bad as you think it is and it's never as good as you think it is," he said.

"I think there's a lot of talent, and without being a super nerd - which rugby pundits often can be - if you look at the stats, we create lots of opportunities.

"When we were on our unbeaten run of 12 games, 83 per cent of the time we got into the 22-metre line, we took away points.

"When we were losing games, we were making the same opportunities but coming away with points less than 33 per cent of the time.

Haskell also praised the ego and style of rising star Henry Pollock.

The Northampton Saints back-row who made headlines by becoming the first rugby union player to sign for Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency back in March, could be given more international chances in the coming weeks.

"He's definitely got that X-factor, in terms of the way he plays," said Haskell.

"He's probably the most talked about rugby player at the moment. He creates opinion and challenges opinion - and that's what makes the world go round now.

"But when he gets opportunities on the field, he delivers… I'm very excited that he will hopefully get more of a chance to play for England.

"It will challenge some of the stuffier, more stoic sides of the upper echelons, and of the fanbase, who like their sports stars manageable and with a bit of ego, but not too much.

"If someone could bring that cohesion together, keep raising awareness and building superstars like Henry Pollock, you're going to be in a great place."

images.caption: Image: Former England back-row James Haskell spoke to Sky Sports about head coach Borthwick and back-row Pollock

articles.title: Nations Championship 2026: How are Ireland set for November Tests?
articles.summary: As Ireland prepare for the northern hemisphere series in the 2026 Nations Championship, BBC Sport NI takes a look at how Andy Farrell's side is shaping up.
articles.body:
The last time Ireland entered an autumn schedule a year out from the Rugby World Cup, Andy Farrell's side were riding the crest of a wave.

Buoyed by their seismic Test series triumph over the All Blacks in New Zealand, Ireland dispatched South Africa, Fiji and Australia to end 2022 top of the world rankings.

At that point, their World Cup preparations were progressing smoothly.

But in the three years since the All Blacks exacted revenge in one of the great World Cup knockout matches in Paris, Ireland's place among rugby's elite has often looked less than assured.

Persistent defeats by New Zealand, South Africa and France have raised questions about the team's trajectory as next year's World Cup draws closer.

But with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa visiting Dublin over the next three weeks, Ireland have the opportunity to give their journey to Australia a much-needed shot in the arm.

Will the Ulsterman with farmer's strength be Ireland's next star?

Ireland 'optimistic' on Prendergast fitness

The aforementioned sequence of poor results against rugby's heavyweights is a key concern.

Ireland have lost their past six meetings with New Zealand, France and South Africa by double-digit margins.

In those six games, they have scored 101 points and conceded 191, while the two most recent reverses - a 36-14 loss away to France in this year's Six Nations and July's 40-21 defeat inside the All Blacks' Eden Park fortress - were the heaviest.

It has not been all gloom, of course. The manner in which Ireland tore through England at Twickenham earlier this year was a thrilling reminder of their big-game prowess.

However, Farrell will be desperate for his side extinguish an error-prone performance in Auckland that allowed New Zealand to effectively wrap up the game by half-time.

To sufficiently alter the narrative, they must avoid first home losses to Argentina and Fiji before renewing hostilities with South Africa.

Last year, the Springboks devoured the Irish scrum in a 24-13 win in Dublin. Landing a knockout blow on the world champions at this stage in the cycle would be a significant statement.

In their quest for revenge, Ireland have placed an even greater emphasis on conditioning, with assistant coach Johnny Sexton saying they want it to be their "point of difference".

Whether that approach bears early fruit this month remains to be seen.

To topple the fearsome South African scrum, Farrell needs his strongest front row, so confirmation of Tadhg Furlong's availability will have been welcomed by the coaching team.

The three-time British and Irish Lions tourist was cleared by a disciplinary committee of grabbing Gavin Coombes in the groin during Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster.

With Furlong and fellow Lion Andrew Porter available, Farrell and scrum coach John Fogarty must devise a masterplan to establish Ireland a dominant set-piece force this month.

But Farrell has issues further back in the pack. With captain Caelan Doris and Jack Conan ruled out, Sean Jansen appears the frontrunner for the number eight jersey, although Dan Sheehan's run-out in the back row against Munster has raised the possibility of a more radical shake-up.

Uncapped Ulsterman James McNabney can fulfil that role, too, although the 23-year-old's recent comments suggest his playing time this month may be limited.

Ryan Baird's return offers another tried-and-tested option at blind-side flanker, with Tadhg Beirne and Cian Prendergast having featured there in the summer.

There is also uncertainty surrounding fly-half Sam Prendergast's fitness, with Jack Crowley already ruled out.

Prendergast has been nursing a wrist problem, and while Ireland said they were "optimistic" he will be available for selection, Ciaran Frawley may be afforded another opportunity at 10 following his impressive start to life at Connacht.

Ulster's Jamie Benson, a former England Under-20 international, is a more unknown quantity in the key playmaker role.

And with the injured Garry Ringrose unlikely to feature in November, Jamie Osborne - who played wing and full-back against Australia and Japan in the summer - could deputise at outside centre if Farrell decides against going for the more experienced Robbie Henshaw.

As for the wings, Mack Hansen's return is a welcome sight for Irish fans.

The 28-year-old, who missed the Six Nations and summer Tests, is a dynamic option out wide or at full-back, having scored a hat-trick of tries in the 15 jersey against Australia last year.

Argentina have never beaten Ireland in Dublin but stunned the British and Irish Lions on their most recent visit to the Aviva Stadium last year.

Pumas head coach Felipe Contepomi has made three changes to his original 33-player squad as Facundo Isa, Rodrigo Martinez and Mateo Soler are late call-ups.

Captain Julian Montoya is one of a number of experienced players to return after missing out on the home defeats by South Africa and Australia in August, plus September's draw away to the Wallabies, but they will be without the injured Santiago Grondona, Ignacio Ruiz and Joaquin Oviedo.

Argentina are also without prop Thomas Gallo and utility back Santi Carreras, who impressed in the win over the Lions.

Those recent Tests saw Contepomi preside over a depleted squad, while in the summer, they suffered home defeats by England and Scotland, but did account for Wales.

Argentina play enterprising, free-flowing rugby but their form has been mixed, making them an intriguing opening opponent.

Fiji were beaten by Scotland, England and Wales during the southern hemisphere leg, but a Test win over Japan in October marked the first game in charge for new head coach Jake White, who led South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007.

White named a 35-strong squad which includes former England number eight Nathan Hughes as one of four uncapped players, while Josua Tuisova, Jiuta Wainiqolo and Caleb Muntz are also included.

Farrell has experimented with his line-up in previous meetings. In 2024, he gave Test debuts to Gus McCarthy and Cormac Izuchukwu in a 52-17 win.

As for South Africa, they may have lost their most recent Test against Australia, but the Springboks are far from crisis mode.

A 3-1 series win over New Zealand and three impressive summer Nations Championship victories on home soil have helped them remain at the world rankings summit.

The world champions will be without some key figures in November with Cheslin Kolbe, Eben Etzebeth, Handre Pollard and Andre Esterhuizen all ruled out through injury.

However, head coach Rassie Erasmus will have captain Siya Kolisi, Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende at his disposal.

He has also included six uncapped players in his squad as preparations for next year's World Cup defence intensify.

Forwards: Ryan Baird, Tadhg Beirne, Billy Bohan, Thomas Clarkson, Tadhg Furlong, Sam Illo, Sean Jansen, Ronan Kelleher, Joe McCarthy, James McNabney, Darragh Murray, Tom O'Toole, Andrew Porter, Cian Prendergast, James Ryan, Dan Sheehan (captain), Tom Stewart, Nick Timoney, Josh van der Flier.

articles.title: Marcus Smith, Finn Russell and Ollie Chessum - Prem talking points
articles.summary: Is Marcus Smith in pole position to start for England at 10 against the Wallabies? And should Finn Russell's trash-talk ball-drop have gone unpunished?
articles.body:
It is 21 months since Marcus Smith last started a match at fly-half for England.

In the wake of an opening-round defeat by Ireland in the 2025 Six Nations, the 27-year-old fell behind Fin Smith and George Ford in race for number 10 and never recovered.

Head coach Steve Borthwick has instead preferred him as a full-back or a versatile replacement option.

After Smith stepped into scrum-half against Fiji in the summer, there was even talk of him covering nine as part of his portfolio.

But a start at 10 – his preferred role and one he played for eight successive Tests before being shunted elsewhere – has not even looked likely.

With first-choice Fin Smith a major doubt after sustaining a calf injury, Marcus Smith is the form fly-half pick to start against Australia on Sunday.

Smith, who missed the opening two Prem games, has been key to Harlequins' recent revival.

His clever support line helped set up a try for Cadan Murley inside two minutes of Saturday's win over Exeter. His late sweep to the blindside overloaded the defence for Jack Kenningham's try at the other end of the contest.

Harlequins were far more ruthless than Chiefs.

The visitors came away with five tries from seven visits to Exeter's 22m. The Chiefs corresponding figure was four from 13.

Smith's leadership was key as he steered his side back from seven points down early in the second half to victory.

That game management will be under the microscope if Smith does get the nod to start against the Wallabies.

Borthwick will also have noted a brewing batch of young English-qualified forwards – two-try Lucas Schmid, second row Elliot Williams and replacement front row Will Hobson, Sam Riley, Ollie Streeter among them – who came together well in a hard-nosed performance.

Quins claim victory at Exeter in nine-try nailbiter

Leicester could easily be sitting pretty, not only at the top of the table, but also with a 100% record.

The 40-38 defeat by Saracens in the opening round - their only Prem loss so far this season - was a game which could have crumbled any which way.

Since then, they have ground their way into first place via some stereotypically forthright performances.

Captain Ollie Chessum has arrived late to this Prem campaign. A foot injury kept him out until last weekend's win over Northampton.

But he has been bristling with intent, embodying Leicester's ethos.

After a grapple with Henry Pollock and others in the East Midlands derby, he briefly got shirty with England team-mate Ellis Genge at Ashton Gate.

Knowing smiles were quickly shared between the pair rather than any flying fists.

But Chessum was a nuisance all night for the Bears, charging down scrum-half Harry Randall in the opening two minutes, wrecking the hosts' line-out, securing a couple of turnovers and bringing his physicality and energy to bear in close quarters.

It was a performance to vindicate a bumper new contract, announced last week.

For their investment, Tigers and coach Geoff Parling have the perfect figurehead to rally around.

Leicester dominate Bristol to go top of the Prem

Unsaid, but perhaps implied, was the suggestion that champions Northampton's free-running, free-scoring style, for all its thrills, would be choked off at source on the international stage.

With referee Sara Cox promoting the contest on the floor, Val Rapava-Ruskin, Jack Clement and Dewi Lake all came up with big jackal turnovers as the visitors went toe to toe with Saints for an hour.

It wasn't until the 34th minute that Northampton made their first inroads into the opposition 22m as their usual flow and cutting edge went missing.

Northampton found a way. Two rolling mauls bought them parity on the half-time scoreboard, and a pair of well-worked final-quarter tries from George Hendy and Rory Hutchinson ensured a bonus-point win.

But after Bristol and Leicester had success with similar approaches earlier this season, coaches Phil Dowson and Sam Vesty can expect more teams to try to target the breakdown and pour sludge into Saints' attacking gears.

Saints rally to beat Gloucester but Mitchell hobbles off injured

The viral moment of the weekend came at The Rec.

Defeat by Gloucester last weekend meant that Bath fly-half Finn Russell had been denied his traditional shushing of the Shed at Kingsholm.

He clearly had some housery to get out of his system.

Midway through the first half, with Bath having just retaken the lead against Sale, Russell gathered George Ford's chip ahead and, as the referee's whistle blew for a penalty for the visitors, bumped the chasing Sale fly-half to the floor with a shoulder to the chest.

A melee ensued. Russell escaped censure.

Referee Anthony Woodthorpe could have punished Russell with a penalty for breaching the spirit of sportsmanship, advancing Sale up the pitch and giving them a shot at a line-out from close range - the source of their only try in the match to that point.

It wouldn't have changed the outcome of the match. Sale failed to capitalise on a similar platform a few minutes later.

But it might discourage such cheap-shot taunts as Russell's.

Or should officials let such things slide as part of the game's rough and tumble?

Cokanasiga scores twice as Bath overcome Sale

Hicks and Red Bulls continue to threaten

Max Hicks produced another big performance in another promising display for Newcastle Red Bulls, this time against Saracens.

The 27-year-old, who was born in Auckland but qualifies for England through his mother, is a back-row triple threat, making gains on the floor (two turnovers), with ball in hand (56m off 11 carries) and at the line-out with quality jumping skills honed during a childhood playing high-level Aussie Rules.

Newcastle led for the majority of the match.

Their hopes of victory were torpedoed by second-half yellow cards for Sam Graham and Alex Hearle. Saracens scored four of their six tries in a 17-minute period with at least a man advantage.

Newcastle go into the international break bottom of the table. It is a familiar position, but they are just a point behind Exeter and Sale and there is a buzz of something building.

Second-half blitz helps Saracens beat Newcastle

Bath back row Miles Reid made an interesting observation earlier this season, suggesting rugby had failed to tap into the sport's classic collared shirts becoming a fashion trend.

While Formula 1 and football have done limited edition high-end collaboration with brands, Reid wondered why rugby has failed to capture the zeitgeist. , external

Bristol revived their old format of using letters, rather than numbers, on the back of their shirts as a one-off for Friday's game against Leicester. , external

Saracens wore an old-school hooped number against Sale last month as part of their 150th anniversary season celebrations.

Prem Rugby got various stars decked out in vintage numbers for their season launch event.

But is there a bold breakthrough still to be made by a club, that could help the game as a whole?

articles.title: Scotland lose Jamie Ritchie and Elliot Millar Mills through injury
articles.summary: Glasgow Warriors flanker Jamie Ritchie and Newcastle Red Bulls prop Elliot Millar Mills drop out of Scotland's Nations Championship squad following picking up injuries for their clubs over the weekend.
articles.body:
Glasgow Warriors flanker Jamie Ritchie and Newcastle Red Bulls prop Elliot Millar Mills have dropped out of Scotland's Nations Championship squad after picking up injuries for their clubs over the weekend.

Uncapped Ollie Blyth-Lafferty, fellow Edinburgh prop D'arcy Rae and back-row clubmate Freddy Douglas have been called up as replacements.

Ritchie, who has 63 caps, joined Glasgow from Perpignan this summer. However, the 30-year-old only made his debut last month after being sidelined for the opening months of the season because of ankle and Achilles tendon issues.

He started in the 24-20 win away to Benetton. But he came off with a knee injury after only 10 minutes of Friday's 29-20 win over Lions that took Glasgow to the top of the United Rugby Championship.

Millar Mills lasted five minutes of Newcastle's 59-26 defeat away to Northampton Saints in England's Premiership before the 34-year-old suffered a leg injury that will delay hopes of adding to his 15 caps.

Meanwhile, Sale Sharks scrum-half Gus Warr, who already has two caps, will join up with the squad for training this week along with uncapped Glasgow back Josh McKay, who is continuing his rehab from a hamstring injury.

Scotland entertain New Zealand on Saturday, 7 November before hosting Australia eight days later, then Japan on 21 November.
